8: ## Abstract
9: 
10: Summary Background Before 2020, mental disorders were leading causes of the global health-related burden, with depressive and anxiety disorders being leading contributors to this burden. The emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic has created an environment where many determinants of poor mental health are exacerbated. The need for up-to-date information on the mental health impacts of COVID-19 in a way that informs health system responses is imperative. In this study, we aimed to quantify the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders globally in 2020. Methods We conducted a systematic review of data reporting the prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and published between Jan 1, 2020, and Jan 29, 2021. We searched PubMed, Google Scholar, preprint servers, grey literature sources, and consulted experts. Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders that were representative of the general population during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used the assembled data in a meta-regression to estimate change in the prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders between pre-pandemic and mid-pandemic (using periods as defined by each study) via COVID-19 impact indicators (human mobility, daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, and daily excess mortality rate). We then used this model to estimate the change from pre-pandemic prevalence (estimated using Disease Modelling Meta-Regression version 2.1 [known as DisMod-MR 2.1]) by age, sex, and location. We used final prevalence estimates and disability weights to estimate years lived with disability and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. 12: Research in context Evidence before this study For our study, we did a systematic literature review of the peer-reviewed and grey literature for studies published between Jan 1, 2020, and Jan 29, 2021, investigating prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic. Most of the identified work consisted of surveys done for a specific location, at a snapshot in time, and indicated an increase in prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic. We also found several systematic reviews and meta-analyses to summarise these studies; however, these studies were either qualitative syntheses or simply presented pooled estimates across studies. We did not find any studies that attempted to synthesise the global prevalence and burden of depressive and anxiety disorders due to the COVID-19 pandemic for the year 2020. Added value of this study This study is the first to quantify the prevalence and burden of depressive and anxiety disorders by age, sex, and location globally. We compiled available evidence of the change in the prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic. We then developed a model to estimate the prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders by age, sex, and location on the basis of available indicators of the location-specific impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. We then used prevalence to estimate the burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders due to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. 14: ## Introduction
15: 
16: Mental disorders are among the leading causes of the global health-related burden. The Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2019 showed that the two most disabling mental disorders were depressive and anxiety disorders, both ranked among the top 25 leading causes of burden worldwide in 2019. 1 , 2 This burden was high across the entire lifespan, for both sexes, and across many locations. 2 Perhaps more importantly, no reduction in the global prevalence or burden was detected for either disorder since 1990, despite compelling evidence of interventions that reduce their impact. 3
17: 
18: The emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 against this backdrop has raised many questions around the resulting effects on mental health via its direct psychological effects and long-term economic and social consequences. 4 COVID-19 continues to spread across most of the world's populations 1 , 2 with significant health consequences and mortality among those who become infected. 5 In addition to the direct effects of COVID-19, the pandemic has created an environment in which many determinants of mental health are also affected. Social restrictions, lockdowns, school and business closures, loss of livelihood, decreases in economic activity, and shifting priorities of governments in their attempt to control COVID-19 outbreaks all have the potential to substantially affect the mental health of the population. The need for up-to-date information on the global prevalence and burden of mental disorders incorporating the mental health impacts of COVID-19 in a way that informs health system responses has never been more urgent.
19: 
20: GBD 2020 is in the process of estimating the burden of 370 diseases and injuries 88 risk factors across 204 countries and territories. GBD 2020 is quantifying the burden using disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), which represent the number of years of healthy life lost to either mortality or disability. Here, as part of GBD 2020, we present a method built on the mental disorder estimates presented in GBD 2019 by incorporating the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic. We quantify the impact of COVID-19 on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders by location, age, and sex in 2020.
21: 
22: ## Methods
23: 
24: ### Overview
25: 
26: First, we conducted a systematic literature review to assemble data from surveys measuring the effect of COVID-19 on the prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders. Second, we used these data in a meta-analysis to (1) estimate the change in prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders before versus during the COVID-19 pandemic, (2) predict (through the use of selected indicators of COVID-19 impact) the resulting change in prevalence of each disorder across all GBD locations, and (3) translate changes in prevalence to corresponding changes in burden estimates as years lived with disability (YLDs) and DALYs. A conceptual overview of this process is shown in the appendix (p 17) . This study complies with the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting (GATHER) recommendations ( appendix pp 26–27 ) 6 and all code used in the analyses can be found online.
27: 
28: ### Case definitions
29: 
30: To ensure comparability in measurement, we used case definitions for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders used within the GBD framework. These definitions adhere to criteria presented in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorder fourth edition text revision (DSM-IV-TR) 7 and the tenth International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-10). 8 Detailed case definitions are in the appendix (p 6) .
31: 
32: ### Data sources
33: 
34: We conducted a systematic literature search to identify population surveys reporting on the prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders, or both, during the COVID-19 pandemic. We used the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines; 9 our PRISMA checklist is in the appendix (pp 28–31 ), and the search protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, CRD42021216590).
35: 
36: We searched for data sources published between Jan 1, 2020, and Jan 29, 2021. The search involved electronic searches of the peer-reviewed literature using PubMed, the grey literature (ie, the COVID-19: living map of the evidence by Eppi-centre , The DEPRESSD Project , Google Scholar, The Neurology and Neuropsychiatry of COVID-19 Blog , the WHO COVID 19 literature database , COVID-Minds , and the MedRxiv and PsyArXiv preprint servers), and expert consultation. Search strings for each search are in the appendix (p 5) . No language restrictions were applied.
37: 
38: Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used timelines for these periods as defined by each study. Prevalence surveys conducted during the pandemic could not be included without comparable pre-pandemic data (ie, using the same instrument, location, and age group) collected since 2013 to assess the change in prevalence. Longitudinal studies using samples representative of the general population were preferred, but cross-sectional studies were also included if comparable pre-pandemic prevalence data existed. Studies using random sampling were preferred; however, due to challenges imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic, there were few studies of this type. Studies using market research quota sampling were also included but were controlled for with a covariate in our analysis. Market research quota sampling is a non-probabilistic sampling strategy whereby participants are identified from a database to match the population of interest (a discussion of the use of these estimates is in the appendix [p 7] ). 10 Samples obtained via this method might produce results that differ from the general population. 11 , 12
39: 
40: Studies reporting probable cases of depressive or anxiety disorders using established screening measures were included due to the paucity of available survey data from during the COVID-19 pandemic using diagnostic instruments. In these instances, only prevalence estimates for cases that reached established thresholds for probable depressive or anxiety disorder were included. We assumed the predictive validity between probable versus diagnosed cases using these screening measures did not change during the COVID-19 pandemic compared with before the pandemic, and therefore the change in the prevalence of probable cases would be equivalent to the change in the prevalence of diagnosed cases (additional discussion of this assumption is in the appendix [pp 8–9] ). We also included measures capturing symptoms of both depressive and anxiety disorders (eg, the K-6 Distress Scale), which were also controlled for with a covariate in analyses. For eligible studies, we extracted information on location, age, sex, prevalence, uncertainty, number of cases, sample size, recall period, disorder, diagnostic instrument, sampling strategy, and dates between which the survey was conducted. We extracted the most detailed data reported by age and sex.
41: 
42: We required indicators of the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic that had an association with prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, hereafter referred to as COVID-19 impact indicators. The risk factor of interest was the COVID-19 pandemic, with the COVID-19 impact indicators acting as proxies for the effect of COVID-19 in the population. A COVID-19 impact indicator had to capture an effect of COVID-19, be consistently measured across locations, and be consistently measured with sufficient granularity across time (preferably daily or weekly) over the course of the pandemic. Our process of selecting the COVID-19 impact indicators is detailed in the appendix (p 10) . Ultimately, we considered three novel indicators of the COVID-19 pandemic: decreasing human mobility, 13 estimated total (as opposed to reported) daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, and estimated daily excess mortality rate during the pandemic (including excess deaths occurring during the pandemic where COVID-19 was not reported as the underlying cause of death). 5 , 13
43: 
44: The estimation of human mobility, daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, and daily excess mortality rate was done by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) COVID-19 Forecasting Team and is described in detail elsewhere. 13 In summary, human mobility was represented by a composite human mobility index representing daily change from pre-pandemic mobility. Data from mobile phone users provided by Facebook, Google, Descartes Labs, Safegraph, and Baidu, and data on physical distancing mandates informed a Gaussian process regression to estimate a time series for human mobility. Daily SARS-CoV-2 infection and excess mortality rates were estimated via a deterministic susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered (known as SEIR) compartmental framework and was informed by daily confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections, COVID-19-related deaths, SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted, antibody seroprevalence, human mobility, physical distancing mandates, pneumonia seasonality, facemask use, and vaccine coverage. 5 , 13
45: 
46: GBD conducts routine systematic reviews of the epidemiology of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders as part of the estimation of YLDs (and separately to the aforementioned systematic review of the change in prevalence due to COVID-19). The compiled epidemiological data for GBD 2020 includes studies done from 1980 to 2019 on the prevalence, incidence, remission, duration, and excess mortality of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. These data were identified through routine electronic searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase, grey literature sources (including a review of the Global Health Data Exchange library), and consultation with experts. GBD 2020 uses Disease Modelling Meta-Regression version 2.1 (known as DisMod-MR 2.1), a Bayesian disease modelling meta-regression tool, to analyse these data and generate internally consistent estimates of prevalence, incidence, remission, and mortality by sex, location, year, and age group for each disorder. 14 It also estimates prevalence for locations that are missing raw epidemiological data. GBD 2020 does this by estimating prevalence across a cascade down five levels of a geographical hierarchy: global, super-region, region, country or territory, and subnational locations. The prevalence from locations higher in the hierarchy act as priors for the prevalence for locations lower in the hierarchy. More detail on DisMod-MR 2.1 and the estimation of prevalence data for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders has been published elsewhere. 1 , 14 Because no epidemiological data from the year 2020 informed the DisMod-MR 2.1 model for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, the prevalence produced for 2020 by age and sex and for each of the 204 countries and territories represented the prevalence of each disorder without the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
47: 
48: We made use of severity distributions and disability weights in GBD 2020 ( appendix p 32 ). We apportioned the final disorder prevalence for the year 2020 into the categories of asymptomatic, mild, moderate, and severe with corresponding disability weights. Disability weights in GBD 2020 quantify health loss from a health state on a scale of 0 (no health loss) to 1 (equivalent to death). The process to estimate severity proportions and disability weights in GBD 2020 has been described elsewhere. 2 , 15
49: 
50: ### Statistical analysis
51: 
52: We estimated the prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic by first developing a model to predict adjustments to pre-pandemic prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders based on COVID-19 impact indicators, and then modifying the pre-pandemic prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders estimated from DisMod-MR 2.1. We conducted meta-regressions, using meta-regression—Bayesian, regularised, trimmed 16 (MR-BRT), on the difference between logit disorder prevalence before the COVID-19 pandemic and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The process to build a final meta-regression model is described in detail in the appendix (pp 6–7 ). Briefly, potential bias covariates that were identified were cross-sectional comparisons informed by random samples, longitudinal comparisons informed by market research and quota samples, cross-sectional comparisons informed by market research and quota samples, and estimates representing combined symptoms of depressive and anxiety disorders ( appendix p 32 ). Because only three studies used diagnostic instruments to measure prevalence, we did not have sufficient data to explore the effect of a bias covariate on data from screening scales identifying probable cases of depressive or anxiety disorders ( appendix pp 8–9 ). Each unique sample was given a random intercept and random effects were placed on the COVID-19 impact indicators. We ran models separately for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. We also included age, sex, and most bias covariates as effect modifiers to ensure that the prevalence change remained zero when the COVID-19 impact was zero. 54: Due to the strong collinearity between the COVID-19 impact indicators (inspected via Pearson correlation coefficients) and the need for age, sex, and bias covariates to be treated as effect modifiers on the impact indicators, we developed prevalence adjustment models via a two-step process. In step one, we used indicator models to develop a so-called index for the impact of COVID-19. Human mobility, daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, and daily excess mortality rate were included simultaneously in a meta-regression on the change in logit prevalence to quantify their independent effect on prevalence change. We used the coefficients from these models to calculate a single COVID-19 impact indicator for each disorder. In step two, we developed a final model for each disorder via backward elimination to regress the COVID-19 impact indicator, age, sex, and the bias covariates on the change in logit prevalence. The least significant covariate was iteratively removed until no improvement was seen in the Akaike information criterion. We assessed the generalisability of the model using a leave-one-country-out cross-validation analysis ( appendix p 11 ).

# Structured Rewrite Based on Published Full Text

**Source:** COVID-19 Mental Disorders Collaborators. *Global prevalence and burden of depressive and anxiety disorders in 204 countries and territories in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.* The Lancet, 2021.
- **DOI:** [10.1016/S0140-6736(21)02143-7](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(21)02143-7)
- **PMCID:** [PMC8500697](https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC8500697)
- **PROSPERO:** CRD42021216590
- **Full text inspected:** Yes (JATS XML via Europe PMC, retrieved 2026-07-18)

> This document is a structured re-expression of the published study. All quantitative results, methodological details, sample sizes, limitations, and conclusions are drawn exclusively from the verified published full text. No content has been inferred from the title or abstract alone.

---

## Abstract

**Background.** Depressive and anxiety disorders were leading contributors to the global health burden before 2020. The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated multiple determinants of poor mental health through social restrictions, economic disruption, and direct psychological effects. This study, conducted as part of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2020, estimated the impact of the pandemic on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders across 204 countries and territories, stratified by age and sex.

**Methods.** A systematic review identified population surveys reporting prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the pandemic (January 2020 to January 2021). Eligible studies required a pre-pandemic baseline using the same instrument, location, and age group. From 5683 unique records, 48 studies met inclusion criteria (46 for major depressive disorder, 27 for anxiety disorders). A Bayesian meta-regression (MR-BRT) modelled the change in logit prevalence as a function of two significant COVID-19 impact indicators—human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate—controlling for age, sex, and sampling bias. Pre-pandemic prevalence estimates were derived from DisMod-MR 2.1 (GBD 2019). Adjusted prevalence was translated to years lived with disability (YLDs) and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) using GBD 2020 severity distributions and disability weights.

**Findings.** After adjustment for the pandemic, global major depressive disorder prevalence rose from 2470.5 per 100 000 (193 million people) to 3152.9 per 100 000 (246 million), yielding an additional 53.2 million cases—a 27.6% increase. Anxiety disorder prevalence rose from 3824.9 per 100 000 (298 million) to 4802.4 per 100 000 (374 million), adding 76.2 million cases—a 25.6% increase. Females experienced larger absolute and relative increases than males for both disorders. Younger age groups were affected more than older age groups. The pandemic imposed an additional 10.7 million DALYs for major depressive disorder and 9.05 million DALYs for anxiety disorders in 2020.

**Interpretation.** The COVID-19 pandemic generated a substantial additional burden of depressive and anxiety disorders worldwide, disproportionately borne by women and young people. Strengthening mental health systems and deploying evidence-based mitigation strategies is an urgent priority.

---

## Introduction

Mental disorders were among the foremost causes of health-related burden globally before 2020. GBD 2019 ranked depressive and anxiety disorders within the top 25 leading causes of burden, with high prevalence persisting across the lifespan, for both sexes, and across many locations. Critically, no reduction in global prevalence or burden had been detected for either disorder since 1990, despite the availability of evidence-based interventions.

The COVID-19 pandemic, emerging against this pre-existing backdrop, raised concerns about its direct psychological effects and its long-term social and economic consequences. In addition to the direct health impacts of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the pandemic disrupted multiple determinants of mental health: social restrictions, lockdowns, school and business closures, loss of livelihood, reduced economic activity, and shifting government priorities. The need for up-to-date, population-level information that could inform health system responses was urgent.

This study, embedded within GBD 2020, built upon the mental disorder estimates from GBD 2019 and incorporated the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic. The aim was to quantify the impact of COVID-19 on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, disaggregated by location, age, and sex, for the year 2020.

---

## Methods

### Study design and systematic review

The analysis proceeded in three stages: (1) a systematic literature review to collect surveys measuring the pandemic's effect on prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders; (2) a meta-regression to estimate prevalence change as a function of COVID-19 impact indicators and to predict adjusted prevalence across all GBD locations; (3) translation of prevalence changes into YLDs and DALYs. The study complied with the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting (GATHER) and followed PRISMA reporting standards. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42021216590).

Case definitions for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders followed DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 criteria as applied in the GBD framework.

The search covered sources published between January 1, 2020, and January 29, 2021, across PubMed, Google Scholar, the Eppi-centre COVID-19 living map, the DEPRESSD Project, the WHO COVID-19 literature database, COVID-Minds, MedRxiv, PsyArXiv, and grey literature, supplemented by expert consultation. No language restrictions were applied.

Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the pandemic and provided a comparable pre-pandemic baseline (same instrument, location, and age group) collected since 2013. Longitudinal studies with representative samples were preferred, but cross-sectional studies were included if comparable pre-pandemic data existed. Given the paucity of diagnostic-instrument surveys during the pandemic, studies using established screening measures to identify probable cases were included, with the assumption that the predictive validity of these instruments remained unchanged from pre-pandemic to pandemic periods. Studies using market research quota sampling were controlled via covariates. Combined symptom measures (e.g., the K-6 Distress Scale) were also included and adjusted for.

From the 5683 unique records identified, 48 studies met inclusion criteria (46 informing major depressive disorder, 27 informing anxiety disorders; one study reported data across two regions). A supplemental search for pre-pandemic baselines contributed an additional 11 studies for major depressive disorder and 7 for anxiety disorders. Most studies came from western Europe (n=22) and high-income North America (n=14), with smaller representations from Australasia (n=5), high-income Asia Pacific (n=5), east Asia (n=2), and central Europe (n=1).

### COVID-19 impact indicators

Three indicators were evaluated as proxies for the pandemic's population-level effect: (1) a composite human mobility index, representing daily change from pre-pandemic mobility (derived from Facebook, Google, Descartes Labs, Safegraph, Baidu mobile-phone data, and physical-distancing mandates, modelled via Gaussian process regression); (2) estimated total daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate (derived from a deterministic SEIR compartmental model informed by confirmed infections, deaths, testing, seroprevalence, mobility, mandates, seasonality, mask use, and vaccine coverage); and (3) estimated daily excess mortality rate.

### Statistical modelling

Meta-regressions were conducted using MR-BRT (meta-regression—Bayesian, regularised, trimmed) on the difference between logit disorder prevalence before and during the pandemic. Due to strong collinearity among the three indicators, a two-step approach was used. In step one, all three indicators were included simultaneously to derive a single COVID-19 impact index weighted by their independent effects. Human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate were significantly associated with prevalence change for both disorders, while daily excess mortality rate was not (attributed to its high collinearity with the other two indicators: *r* = 0.8 with each). In step two, backward elimination produced a final model regressing the COVID-19 impact index, age, sex, and bias covariates on the logit-prevalence change.

Bias covariates examined included: cross-sectional comparisons with random samples, longitudinal comparisons with market research/quota samples, cross-sectional comparisons with market research/quota samples, and combined-symptom measures. Cross-sectional market research/quota samples significantly overestimated prevalence increases for both disorders and were retained in the final models. The combined-symptom covariate was retained in the anxiety disorders model only. Other bias covariates were not significant and were dropped.

The final models were used to predict daily prevalence changes via Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation (1000 samples), adjusting DisMod-MR 2.1 pre-pandemic estimates for 204 countries and territories. Adjusted prevalence was apportioned into asymptomatic, mild, moderate, and severe categories using GBD 2020 severity distributions with corresponding disability weights. YLDs and DALYs were computed, with DALYs for these disorders consisting entirely of YLDs (neither disorder was classified as an underlying cause of death under ICD rules). Comorbidity corrections were applied. Results are reported with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs), representing the 25th and 975th ranked draws across simulations.

Pre-pandemic prevalence estimates came from DisMod-MR 2.1, a Bayesian meta-regression tool that synthesises epidemiological data (1980–2019) and generates internally consistent estimates by location, year, age, and sex across a five-level geographical hierarchy.

All analyses were conducted in R (version 3.6.3), DisMod-MR 2.1, and MR-BRT.

### Geographical coverage and study characteristics

The 48 included studies were predominantly from high-income settings. The geographical distribution was: western Europe (22 studies), high-income North America (14), Australasia (5), high-income Asia Pacific (5), east Asia (2), and central Europe (1). Only three of the included studies used diagnostic instruments to measure prevalence; the remainder relied on screening scales for probable cases.

---

## Results

### Model estimates

In the indicator model, human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate were both significantly associated with prevalence change for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. Daily excess mortality rate was not significant after controlling for the other two indicators.

The final model showed that increasing COVID-19 impact (the combined index) was associated with increased prevalence of major depressive disorder (coefficient 0.4, 95% UI 0.1–0.6) and anxiety disorders (0.4, 95% UI 0.3–0.5). For both disorders, the effect was stronger in females than males and stronger in younger than older age groups. Cross-sectional market research/quota samples overestimated the prevalence increase for both major depressive disorder (0.9, 95% UI 0.6–1.2) and anxiety disorders (0.6, 95% UI 0.2–1.0).

### Prevalence of major depressive disorder

Before adjustment for the pandemic, estimated global major depressive disorder prevalence in 2020 was 2470.5 cases (95% UI 2143.5–2870.7) per 100 000 population, corresponding to 193 million people (95% UI 167–224 million). After adjustment, prevalence rose to 3152.9 cases (95% UI 2722.5–3654.5) per 100 000, or 246 million people (95% UI 212–285 million). The pandemic was estimated to have caused an additional 53.2 million cases (95% UI 44.8–62.9 million), representing an increase of 27.6% (95% UI 25.1–30.3%).

The increase was greater in females than males: 35.5 million additional cases among females (912.5 per 100 000 females; a 29.8% increase) versus 17.7 million additional cases among males (453.6 per 100 000 males; a 24.0% increase).

### Prevalence of anxiety disorders

Pre-pandemic estimated global anxiety disorder prevalence was 3824.9 cases (95% UI 3283.3–4468.1) per 100 000, equivalent to 298 million people (95% UI 256–348 million). After adjustment, prevalence reached 4802.4 cases (95% UI 4108.2–5588.6) per 100 000, or 374 million people (95% UI 320–436 million). The additional caseload attributed to the pandemic was 76.2 million (95% UI 64.3–90.6 million), an increase of 25.6% (95% UI 23.2–28.0%).

Again, females bore a disproportionate burden: 51.8 million additional cases among females (1332.1 per 100 000 females; a 27.9% increase) compared with 24.4 million among males (625.0 per 100 000 males; a 21.7% increase).

### DALY burden

For major depressive disorder, baseline DALYs were 38.7 million (95% UI 26.4–53.9 million) globally, rising to 49.4 million (95% UI 33.6–68.7 million) after pandemic adjustment. The addition was 10.7 million DALYs (95% UI 7.21–14.9 million), with 7.07 million among females and 3.62 million among males. The global additional DALY rate was 137.1 per 100 000 (182.0 per 100 000 females; 92.5 per 100 000 males).

For anxiety disorders, baseline DALYs were 35.5 million (95% UI 23.9–50.1 million), increasing to 44.5 million (95% UI 30.2–62.5 million) post-adjustment. The pandemic contributed 9.05 million additional DALYs (95% UI 6.18–12.8 million), with 6.11 million among females and 2.94 million among males. The global additional DALY rate was 116.1 per 100 000 (157.2 per 100 000 females; 75.3 per 100 000 males).

---

## Discussion

This study provides the first systematic global quantification of the COVID-19 pandemic's impact on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, disaggregated by location, age, and sex for the year 2020. The estimated increases were substantial—an additional 53.2 million cases of major depressive disorder and 76.2 million cases of anxiety disorders—with corresponding additional DALYs of 10.7 million and 9.05 million respectively.

Countries that experienced the most severe pandemic impacts during 2020, as captured by reduced human mobility and elevated SARS-CoV-2 infection rates, were estimated to have the greatest increases in disorder prevalence. The two indicators should be understood as proxies for the broader effects of the pandemic, not as independent risk factors. They incorporated the combined consequences of viral spread, lockdowns, stay-at-home orders, reduced public transport, school and business closures, and diminished social interaction.

The larger increase in prevalence among females is consistent with the understanding that women were disproportionately affected by the pandemic's social and economic consequences: additional caregiving responsibilities during school closures, financial disadvantage from lower salaries and less secure employment, and increased rates of domestic violence during periods of lockdown. The larger increase among younger age groups likewise aligns with known mechanisms: UNESCO estimated 1.6 billion learners in over 190 countries were fully or partially out of school in 2020, and young people face higher unemployment risk during economic crises.

The findings echo prior evidence on how population shocks elevate common mental disorders. After the 2009 financial crisis, for example, major depressive episode prevalence in Greece rose from 3.3% (2008) to 8.2% (2011), and in Hong Kong from 8.2% (2007) to 12.5% (2009). The magnitude and time course differ across studies, reflecting varying combinations of health and socioeconomic determinants.

The relationship between increased disorder prevalence and suicide trends remains uncertain. While an early study of 21 countries found no significant increase in suicide rates between April and July 2020, another analysis from Japan showed a 14% decrease during the first five months of the pandemic followed by a 16% increase in the subsequent four months, with larger effects among females and younger populations. The present study had insufficient data to draw conclusions on this matter.

Even before the pandemic, mental health systems in most countries were under-resourced and disorganised. The added demand from COVID-19 compounds these pre-existing deficits. Strategies to reduce viral transmission have also made it harder to obtain medication, attend treatment facilities, and receive in-person care. Mitigation strategies should promote mental wellbeing, target determinants of poor mental health exacerbated by the pandemic, and provide accessible treatment pathways—incorporating digital, telehealth, and face-to-face modalities.

### Limitations (as stated by the authors)

The authors identified the following limitations:

1. **Indicator coverage.** Human mobility and SARS-CoV-2 infection rates are unlikely to have captured the full mental health impact across all GBD locations. The precision of these indicators varies, particularly in settings where infection reporting is inconsistent or where disadvantaged subgroups have limited access to the mobile-phone tracking data underpinning the mobility index. Some subgroups cannot reduce their mobility due to employment type, which may distort estimates.

2. **Geographical imbalance in source data.** Very few surveys meeting inclusion criteria came from low-income and middle-income countries. The regression findings may therefore be less generalisable to those locations.

3. **Reliance on screening instruments.** Only three of the 48 studies used diagnostic instruments. The analysis assumed that the predictive validity of screening questionnaires for identifying probable cases did not change from pre-pandemic to pandemic periods. The authors noted this assumption could not be empirically tested with the available data and requires scrutiny in future work.

4. **Undifferentiated infection status.** The estimates did not distinguish between individuals with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. Emerging evidence at the time of writing suggested that post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 might contribute to depressive and anxiety symptoms, making long-COVID prevalence a potential future indicator.

### Research directions

The authors called for high-quality surveys during the pandemic from under-represented regions, with researchers aligning sample frames and mental health measures with pre-pandemic baselines. Where feasible, diagnostic instruments should be included alongside screening questionnaires to enable validation of the predictive-validity assumption and to explore possible shifts in severity distributions among diagnosed individuals.

---

## Source Fidelity Statement

All quantitative values, methodological specifications, study counts, effect sizes, uncertainty intervals, limitations, and conclusions in this document were verified against the published full text (PMC8500697, JATS XML retrieved via Europe PMC on 2026-07-18). No content was fabricated from title or abstract metadata. Items that the source does not report—such as specific country-level prevalence tables, code repository URL, citation counts, or preprint identifiers—are not described as known facts.

---

# Structured Rewrite Based on Published Full Text

**Source:** COVID-19 Mental Disorders Collaborators. *Global prevalence and burden of depressive and anxiety disorders in 204 countries and territories in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.* The Lancet, 2021.
- **DOI:** [10.1016/S0140-6736(21)02143-7](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(21)02143-7)
- **PMCID:** [PMC8500697](https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC8500697)
- **PROSPERO:** CRD42021216590
- **Full text inspected:** Yes (JATS XML via Europe PMC, retrieved 2026-07-18)

> This document is a structured re-expression of the published study. All quantitative results, methodological details, sample sizes, limitations, and conclusions are drawn exclusively from the verified published full text. No content has been inferred from the title or abstract alone.

---

## Abstract

**Background.** Depressive and anxiety disorders were leading contributors to the global health burden before 2020. The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated multiple determinants of poor mental health through social restrictions, economic disruption, and direct psychological effects. This study, conducted as part of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2020, estimated the impact of the pandemic on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders across 204 countries and territories, stratified by age and sex.

**Methods.** A systematic review identified population surveys reporting prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the pandemic (January 2020 to January 2021). Eligible studies required a pre-pandemic baseline using the same instrument, location, and age group. From 5683 unique records, 48 studies met inclusion criteria (46 for major depressive disorder, 27 for anxiety disorders). A Bayesian meta-regression (MR-BRT) modelled the change in logit prevalence as a function of two significant COVID-19 impact indicators—human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate—controlling for age, sex, and sampling bias. Pre-pandemic prevalence estimates were derived from DisMod-MR 2.1 (GBD 2019). Adjusted prevalence was translated to years lived with disability (YLDs) and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) using GBD 2020 severity distributions and disability weights.

**Findings.** After adjustment for the pandemic, global major depressive disorder prevalence rose from 2470.5 per 100 000 (193 million people) to 3152.9 per 100 000 (246 million), yielding an additional 53.2 million cases—a 27.6% increase. Anxiety disorder prevalence rose from 3824.9 per 100 000 (298 million) to 4802.4 per 100 000 (374 million), adding 76.2 million cases—a 25.6% increase. Females experienced larger absolute and relative increases than males for both disorders. Younger age groups were affected more than older age groups. The pandemic imposed an additional 10.7 million DALYs for major depressive disorder and 9.05 million DALYs for anxiety disorders in 2020.

**Interpretation.** The COVID-19 pandemic generated a substantial additional burden of depressive and anxiety disorders worldwide, disproportionately borne by women and young people. Strengthening mental health systems and deploying evidence-based mitigation strategies is an urgent priority.

---

## Introduction

Mental disorders were among the foremost causes of health-related burden globally before 2020. GBD 2019 ranked depressive and anxiety disorders within the top 25 leading causes of burden, with high prevalence persisting across the lifespan, for both sexes, and across many locations. Critically, no reduction in global prevalence or burden had been detected for either disorder since 1990, despite the availability of evidence-based interventions.

The COVID-19 pandemic, emerging against this pre-existing backdrop, raised concerns about its direct psychological effects and its long-term social and economic consequences. In addition to the direct health impacts of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the pandemic disrupted multiple determinants of mental health: social restrictions, lockdowns, school and business closures, loss of livelihood, reduced economic activity, and shifting government priorities. The need for up-to-date, population-level information that could inform health system responses was urgent.

This study, embedded within GBD 2020, built upon the mental disorder estimates from GBD 2019 and incorporated the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic. The aim was to quantify the impact of COVID-19 on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, disaggregated by location, age, and sex, for the year 2020.

---

## Methods

### Study design and systematic review

The analysis proceeded in three stages: (1) a systematic literature review to collect surveys measuring the pandemic's effect on prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders; (2) a meta-regression to estimate prevalence change as a function of COVID-19 impact indicators and to predict adjusted prevalence across all GBD locations; (3) translation of prevalence changes into YLDs and DALYs. The study complied with the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting (GATHER) and followed PRISMA reporting standards. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42021216590).

Case definitions for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders followed DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 criteria as applied in the GBD framework.

The search covered sources published between January 1, 2020, and January 29, 2021, across PubMed, Google Scholar, the Eppi-centre COVID-19 living map, the DEPRESSD Project, the WHO COVID-19 literature database, COVID-Minds, MedRxiv, PsyArXiv, and grey literature, supplemented by expert consultation. No language restrictions were applied.

Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the pandemic and provided a comparable pre-pandemic baseline (same instrument, location, and age group) collected since 2013. Longitudinal studies with representative samples were preferred, but cross-sectional studies were included if comparable pre-pandemic data existed. Given the paucity of diagnostic-instrument surveys during the pandemic, studies using established screening measures to identify probable cases were included, with the assumption that the predictive validity of these instruments remained unchanged from pre-pandemic to pandemic periods. Studies using market research quota sampling were controlled via covariates. Combined symptom measures (e.g., the K-6 Distress Scale) were also included and adjusted for.

From the 5683 unique records identified, 48 studies met inclusion criteria (46 informing major depressive disorder, 27 informing anxiety disorders; one study reported data across two regions). A supplemental search for pre-pandemic baselines contributed an additional 11 studies for major depressive disorder and 7 for anxiety disorders. Most studies came from western Europe (n=22) and high-income North America (n=14), with smaller representations from Australasia (n=5), high-income Asia Pacific (n=5), east Asia (n=2), and central Europe (n=1).

### COVID-19 impact indicators

Three indicators were evaluated as proxies for the pandemic's population-level effect: (1) a composite human mobility index, representing daily change from pre-pandemic mobility (derived from Facebook, Google, Descartes Labs, Safegraph, Baidu mobile-phone data, and physical-distancing mandates, modelled via Gaussian process regression); (2) estimated total daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate (derived from a deterministic SEIR compartmental model informed by confirmed infections, deaths, testing, seroprevalence, mobility, mandates, seasonality, mask use, and vaccine coverage); and (3) estimated daily excess mortality rate.

### Statistical modelling

Meta-regressions were conducted using MR-BRT (meta-regression—Bayesian, regularised, trimmed) on the difference between logit disorder prevalence before and during the pandemic. Due to strong collinearity among the three indicators, a two-step approach was used. In step one, all three indicators were included simultaneously to derive a single COVID-19 impact index weighted by their independent effects. Human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate were significantly associated with prevalence change for both disorders, while daily excess mortality rate was not (attributed to its high collinearity with the other two indicators: *r* = 0.8 with each). In step two, backward elimination produced a final model regressing the COVID-19 impact index, age, sex, and bias covariates on the logit-prevalence change.

Bias covariates examined included: cross-sectional comparisons with random samples, longitudinal comparisons with market research/quota samples, cross-sectional comparisons with market research/quota samples, and combined-symptom measures. Cross-sectional market research/quota samples significantly overestimated prevalence increases for both disorders and were retained in the final models. The combined-symptom covariate was retained in the anxiety disorders model only. Other bias covariates were not significant and were dropped.

The final models were used to predict daily prevalence changes via Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation (1000 samples), adjusting DisMod-MR 2.1 pre-pandemic estimates for 204 countries and territories. Adjusted prevalence was apportioned into asymptomatic, mild, moderate, and severe categories using GBD 2020 severity distributions with corresponding disability weights. YLDs and DALYs were computed, with DALYs for these disorders consisting entirely of YLDs (neither disorder was classified as an underlying cause of death under ICD rules). Comorbidity corrections were applied. Results are reported with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs), representing the 25th and 975th ranked draws across simulations.

Pre-pandemic prevalence estimates came from DisMod-MR 2.1, a Bayesian meta-regression tool that synthesises epidemiological data (1980–2019) and generates internally consistent estimates by location, year, age, and sex across a five-level geographical hierarchy.

All analyses were conducted in R (version 3.6.3), DisMod-MR 2.1, and MR-BRT.

### Geographical coverage and study characteristics

The 48 included studies were predominantly from high-income settings. The geographical distribution was: western Europe (22 studies), high-income North America (14), Australasia (5), high-income Asia Pacific (5), east Asia (2), and central Europe (1). Only three of the included studies used diagnostic instruments to measure prevalence; the remainder relied on screening scales for probable cases.

---

## Results

### Model estimates

In the indicator model, human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate were both significantly associated with prevalence change for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. Daily excess mortality rate was not significant after controlling for the other two indicators.

The final model showed that increasing COVID-19 impact (the combined index) was associated with increased prevalence of major depressive disorder (coefficient 0.4, 95% UI 0.1–0.6) and anxiety disorders (0.4, 95% UI 0.3–0.5). For both disorders, the effect was stronger in females than males and stronger in younger than older age groups. Cross-sectional market research/quota samples overestimated the prevalence increase for both major depressive disorder (0.9, 95% UI 0.6–1.2) and anxiety disorders (0.6, 95% UI 0.2–1.0).

### Prevalence of major depressive disorder

Before adjustment for the pandemic, estimated global major depressive disorder prevalence in 2020 was 2470.5 cases (95% UI 2143.5–2870.7) per 100 000 population, corresponding to 193 million people (95% UI 167–224 million). After adjustment, prevalence rose to 3152.9 cases (95% UI 2722.5–3654.5) per 100 000, or 246 million people (95% UI 212–285 million). The pandemic was estimated to have caused an additional 53.2 million cases (95% UI 44.8–62.9 million), representing an increase of 27.6% (95% UI 25.1–30.3%).

The increase was greater in females than males: 35.5 million additional cases among females (912.5 per 100 000 females; a 29.8% increase) versus 17.7 million additional cases among males (453.6 per 100 000 males; a 24.0% increase).

### Prevalence of anxiety disorders

Pre-pandemic estimated global anxiety disorder prevalence was 3824.9 cases (95% UI 3283.3–4468.1) per 100 000, equivalent to 298 million people (95% UI 256–348 million). After adjustment, prevalence reached 4802.4 cases (95% UI 4108.2–5588.6) per 100 000, or 374 million people (95% UI 320–436 million). The additional caseload attributed to the pandemic was 76.2 million (95% UI 64.3–90.6 million), an increase of 25.6% (95% UI 23.2–28.0%).

Again, females bore a disproportionate burden: 51.8 million additional cases among females (1332.1 per 100 000 females; a 27.9% increase) compared with 24.4 million among males (625.0 per 100 000 males; a 21.7% increase).

### DALY burden

For major depressive disorder, baseline DALYs were 38.7 million (95% UI 26.4–53.9 million) globally, rising to 49.4 million (95% UI 33.6–68.7 million) after pandemic adjustment. The addition was 10.7 million DALYs (95% UI 7.21–14.9 million), with 7.07 million among females and 3.62 million among males. The global additional DALY rate was 137.1 per 100 000 (182.0 per 100 000 females; 92.5 per 100 000 males).

For anxiety disorders, baseline DALYs were 35.5 million (95% UI 23.9–50.1 million), increasing to 44.5 million (95% UI 30.2–62.5 million) post-adjustment. The pandemic contributed 9.05 million additional DALYs (95% UI 6.18–12.8 million), with 6.11 million among females and 2.94 million among males. The global additional DALY rate was 116.1 per 100 000 (157.2 per 100 000 females; 75.3 per 100 000 males).

---

## Discussion

This study provides the first systematic global quantification of the COVID-19 pandemic's impact on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, disaggregated by location, age, and sex for the year 2020. The estimated increases were substantial—an additional 53.2 million cases of major depressive disorder and 76.2 million cases of anxiety disorders—with corresponding additional DALYs of 10.7 million and 9.05 million respectively.

Countries that experienced the most severe pandemic impacts during 2020, as captured by reduced human mobility and elevated SARS-CoV-2 infection rates, were estimated to have the greatest increases in disorder prevalence. The two indicators should be understood as proxies for the broader effects of the pandemic, not as independent risk factors. They incorporated the combined consequences of viral spread, lockdowns, stay-at-home orders, reduced public transport, school and business closures, and diminished social interaction.

The larger increase in prevalence among females is consistent with the understanding that women were disproportionately affected by the pandemic's social and economic consequences: additional caregiving responsibilities during school closures, financial disadvantage from lower salaries and less secure employment, and increased rates of domestic violence during periods of lockdown. The larger increase among younger age groups likewise aligns with known mechanisms: UNESCO estimated 1.6 billion learners in over 190 countries were fully or partially out of school in 2020, and young people face higher unemployment risk during economic crises.

The findings echo prior evidence on how population shocks elevate common mental disorders. After the 2009 financial crisis, for example, major depressive episode prevalence in Greece rose from 3.3% (2008) to 8.2% (2011), and in Hong Kong from 8.2% (2007) to 12.5% (2009). The magnitude and time course differ across studies, reflecting varying combinations of health and socioeconomic determinants.

The relationship between increased disorder prevalence and suicide trends remains uncertain. While an early study of 21 countries found no significant increase in suicide rates between April and July 2020, another analysis from Japan showed a 14% decrease during the first five months of the pandemic followed by a 16% increase in the subsequent four months, with larger effects among females and younger populations. The present study had insufficient data to draw conclusions on this matter.

Even before the pandemic, mental health systems in most countries were under-resourced and disorganised. The added demand from COVID-19 compounds these pre-existing deficits. Strategies to reduce viral transmission have also made it harder to obtain medication, attend treatment facilities, and receive in-person care. Mitigation strategies should promote mental wellbeing, target determinants of poor mental health exacerbated by the pandemic, and provide accessible treatment pathways—incorporating digital, telehealth, and face-to-face modalities.

### Limitations (as stated by the authors)

The authors identified the following limitations:

1. **Indicator coverage.** Human mobility and SARS-CoV-2 infection rates are unlikely to have captured the full mental health impact across all GBD locations. The precision of these indicators varies, particularly in settings where infection reporting is inconsistent or where disadvantaged subgroups have limited access to the mobile-phone tracking data underpinning the mobility index. Some subgroups cannot reduce their mobility due to employment type, which may distort estimates.

2. **Geographical imbalance in source data.** Very few surveys meeting inclusion criteria came from low-income and middle-income countries. The regression findings may therefore be less generalisable to those locations.

3. **Reliance on screening instruments.** Only three of the 48 studies used diagnostic instruments. The analysis assumed that the predictive validity of screening questionnaires for identifying probable cases did not change from pre-pandemic to pandemic periods. The authors noted this assumption could not be empirically tested with the available data and requires scrutiny in future work.

4. **Undifferentiated infection status.** The estimates did not distinguish between individuals with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. Emerging evidence at the time of writing suggested that post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 might contribute to depressive and anxiety symptoms, making long-COVID prevalence a potential future indicator.

### Research directions

The authors called for high-quality surveys during the pandemic from under-represented regions, with researchers aligning sample frames and mental health measures with pre-pandemic baselines. Where feasible, diagnostic instruments should be included alongside screening questionnaires to enable validation of the predictive-validity assumption and to explore possible shifts in severity distributions among diagnosed individuals.
